To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) antiretrovials without HIV infection can cause adverse effects and mitochondrial toxicity; (b) the combination of a protease inhibitor and a nucleoside analog (Zidovudine + Lamivudine) is more toxic than a protease inhibitor plus a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor and a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptas inhibitor (Tenofovir + Emtricitabine) in healthy subjects.
antiretrovial treatment in non-infected patients may lead to subclinical mitochondrial damage.
HIV PEP is associated with mitochondrial toxicity, and the use of Zidovudin-containing regimens is associated with a higher risk for drug discontinuance and mitochondrial toxicity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of mitochondrial toxicogenomics to assess HIV post-exposure treatment toxicity.
mitochondrial toxicogenomics and antiretrovials, which are relevant for HIV management and prevention.
the use of mtDNA as a biomarker of toxicity and the development of new therapeutic alternatives for HIV post-exposure treatment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of PIs plus AZT + FTC or TDF + FTC for PEP is not associated with significant mitochondrial damage, but the use of AZT plus 3TC should be avoided.
PEP is safe and well-tolerated, but the choice of a safer and less-toxic PEP regimen may be a good alternative for patients with a high risk of adverse effects.

PEP is a valuable strategy to prevent further HIV infection, but it is not without risk, especially in those patients with a history of liver disease or other conditions that can affect mitochondrial function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of AZT in the HIV post-exposure setting is not advisable.
the use of antiretrovials without HIV infection may cause mitochondrial toxicity, but this toxicity can be avoided with a proper hepatic metabolism.
HIV PEP may cause mitochondrial toxicity in non-infested subjects, but the use of TDF/FTC instead of AZT/3TC can reduce this risk.
The main takeaway from our work is that
antiretrovials may have a direct effect on mitochondria and that the use of AZT in the treatment of HIV should be carefully monitored.
antiretrovials are still a double-edged sword, with a potential for benefit in the case of PEP but with the risk of causing mitochondrial damage and toxicity.
mitochondrial toxicity should not be overlooked when designing new therapeutic regimens.
